DESC: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on the nature of property/easement requirement. For greenfield work it is expected that the project proponent will not choose site with high environmental offset risks. Such factors should be mitigated by considering prudent/alternate location options.
NT: This choice adjust the already made environmental offset cost estimate in the building blocks by some degree commensurating with the site. This is to compensate for unavoidable impacts on significant environmental matters (e.g. valuable species and ecosystems) on one site, by securing or paying for land at another site, and for managing that land over a period of time, to replace those significant environmental matters which were lost.

DESC: This unknown risk factor should be chosen if compiling early stage (Class 5b) cost estimate for project network elements using concept level scoping with no site-specific review or TNSP input. We expect this to be the most common usage of the TCD. This factor attempts to compensate the accuracy offset (underestimation) observed in the early stage cost estimate of recent NEM projects due to scope creep in the project definition as it matures to advance stage.
NT:
Examples of scope creep in a station project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	Road improvements / access tracks not considered in early stages
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

DESC: This unknown risk factor should be chosen if compiling early stage (Class 5a) cost estimate for project network elements using screening level scoping including high level site-specific review and TNSP input. NT:
Examples of scope creep in a station project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	Road improvements / access tracks not considered in early stages
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

DESC: Do not choose this unknown risk factor if only compiling early stage (Class 5) cost estimate for network elements using the provided building block estimates in this TCD and with limited attribute and risk information. This unknown risk factor is to be used only when the user has an improved knowledge of scope of work and site specific attribute and risk profile resulting in bespoke and confident scope of work. It is expected that such knowledge will result in more varieties and quantities of assets than estimating with Class 5 knowledge (i.e. the magnitude of known cost is more at this stage). For e.g. the station now includes bespoke configuration of switchbay with additional/more surge arrestors than allowed for in the standard building block in the TCD. This factor attempts to compensate the accuracy offset (underestimation) observed in the Class 4 cost estimate of recent NEM projects due to scope creep in the project definition as it matures to advance stage.
NT:
Examples of scope creep in a station project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	Road improvements / access tracks not considered in early stages
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

DESC: Do not choose this unknown risk factor if only compiling early stage (Class 5) cost estimate for network elements using the provided building block estimates in this TCD and with limited attribute and risk information. This unknown risk factor is to be used only when the user has an advance knowledge of scope of work and site specific attribute and risk profile resulting in bespoke and definitive scope of work. It is expected that such knowledge will result in even more varieties and quantities of assets than estimating with Class 4 knowledge (i.e. the magnitude of known cost is even more at this stage). For e.g. the station now includes bigger car park area than allowed for in the standard building block in the TCD. At Class 3, this factor is negligible and it is expected that such scope creep does not remain unknown. A very small correction factor is applied as the project has now matured and the scope is now deemed advance.
NT:
Examples of scope creep in a station project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	Road improvements / access tracks not considered in early stages
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

DESC: Class 1/2 estimate represents 'contractual' cost and is beyond the scope of the TCD. At this stage, it is expected that all the unknown risk factors have materialised, mitigated or avoided and that there are no surprises left in the project. No factor is applied to the compiled cost estimate.
